The Red comb star Astropecten aranciacus initiates its life cycle through broadcast fertilisation, with external gamete union resulting in fertilised ova of microscopic dimensions. The resulting planktonic bipinnaria larvae develop after the absorption of yolk reserves, and these free-swimming larvae undergo progressive yolk utilization until they reach the metamorphic climax. At the point of zygote formation, the estimated wet weight at birth is 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of approximately 200 micrometres, which yields a sphere-volume mass of about 4.2 micrograms. This remarkably small initial mass is characteristic of echinoderms that produce vast numbers of tiny eggs dispersed into the water column. Following a period of planktotrophic feeding in the water column, the bipinnaria larva develops the adult rudiment and prepares for the larval-juvenile transition. The metamorphic transformation itself culminates when the individual reaches a wet weight at metamorphosis of 0.0225 grams , calculated from a diameter of 2.87 millimetres and an estimated height of one millimetre. This ten-thousand-fold increase in mass from the egg stage reflects the substantial feeding activity undertaken during the planktonic phase.

The timing of larval development in Astropecten aranciacus has been investigated under controlled laboratory conditions. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis was recorded at 80 days since birth . This relatively prolonged larval duration suggests that the bipinnaria stages require substantial feeding time to accumulate the necessary energy reserves for the dramatic morphological transformation into a benthic juvenile. The temperature of 14 °C is within the typical winter range for this Mediterranean-dwelling species, and larval development at cooler temperatures may be slower than at summer maxima. Following metamorphosis, the recently metamorphosed juvenile begins its benthic existence, preying upon small molluscs and crustaceans in sandy substrata. Growth during the juvenile phase proceeds steadily as the starfish accumulates biomass and increases in arm length. The sub-adult period is characterised by continued feeding and gradual increases in both disc diameter and arm number, with the gonads remaining in an undeveloped state until a threshold body size is attained.

Sexual maturation in the Red comb star occurs after a substantial period of somatic growth, with the onset of gametogenesis marking the transition to reproductive viability. Under the same thermal conditions of 14 °C [T = 14 °C] that characterise its developmental period, the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at approximately 547.5 days since birth [tp = approximately 547.5 days since birth]. This value, equivalent to about one and a half years, corresponds to the point at which individuals achieve a wet weight at puberty of 94 grams [Wwp = 94 grams]. The relationship between body size and reproductive maturity is consistent with patterns observed in other Astropecten species, where a minimum mass threshold must be attained before gonadal tissue begins to differentiate. At this size, the starfish has a radius of approximately 11.5 millimetres, and the allometric relationship between disc diameter and wet weight yields this pubertal mass. Once gametogenesis commences, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches 50% [GSI = 50%] at 14 °C [T = 14 °C].

As adults continue to grow beyond the pubertal threshold, they eventually approach their maximum possible size, with the ultimate wet weight recorded at 500 grams [Wwi = 500 grams]. This asymptotic mass represents the ceiling of the growth trajectory for the species and is consistent with maximum radius values observed in the field. The lifespan of Astropecten aranciacus reaches approximately 1825 days [am = approximately 1825 days] when maintained at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], which is equivalent to about five years. This longevity is comparable to that of other temperate-water starfish species, though somewhat shorter than the lifespan of deep-water or polar congeners. The five-year maximum lifespan (5 years) [am = 5 years] under these conditions suggests a life history strategy characterised by moderate growth rates and a relatively prolonged reproductive window following the attainment of sexual maturity at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. Field surveys and laboratory observations both confirm that individuals remain reproductively active for several years before entering a phase of reproductive senescence.

The ecological role of Astropecten aranciacus within its sandy-bottom Mediterranean habitat is that of an active predator, with adult individuals preying preferentially on bivalve molluscs. The feeding behaviour involves everting the cardiac stomach over the prey and digesting the soft tissues externally, after which the starfish moves on, leaving empty shells. This predatory pressure can significantly structure the local infaunal community, especially in seagrass meadows and unvegetated soft sediments. Comparative studies with other members of the Astropectinidae reveal that Astropecten aranciacus is one of the larger representatives of the genus, with the 500 gram [Wwi = 500 gram] ultimate wet weight being substantially greater than that of sympatric species such as Astropecten irregularis. The ecological implications of this large body size include a broader prey size spectrum and higher daily food intake rates. Additionally, the five-year maximum lifespan (5 years) [am = 5 years] at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] allows for multiple reproductive episodes, which may buffer the population against recruitment failure in years with poor larval survival. Conservation concerns for this species are minimal at present, but ongoing climate change may alter the thermal regime of the Mediterranean basin, potentially shifting the optimal temperature window for both larval development and adult reproductive physiology.
